newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cannes top prize takes Japan director by surprise.
newsitem.headline: Cannes top prize takes Japan director by surprise.

text.p: The Japanese director whose film took the Golden Palm at the Cannes Film Festival said on Monday he had left France and returned home before the awards ceremony because he felt he had no chance of winning.
Director Shohei Imamura, 70, said he was surprised by the success of his film "Unagi" ("The Eel").
The film shared the festival's top award with the Iranian film, "The Taste of the Cherry".

Imamura said he left Cannes for Tokyo before the award was announced because he thought his film had no chance of winning the coveted top prize at the prestigious French Riviera film festival on Sunday.
"I came back to Tokyo and drank sake because I didn't expect to get it," Imamura said.
"It feels really strange. When I heard the news I thought: Surely not! I really didn't think I would win," Imamura told the Japanese newspaper Asahi Shimbun.
"Many in the audience understood the humour in 'Unagi' and were moved by it. But I really have no idea what aspects of the film the judges valued so highly," he said.

"Unagi" tells the story of Takuro, unrepentant after eight years in jail for stabbing his unfaithful wife to death. He speaks to no one about his true feelings except an eel he catches while in prison.
On his release he meets a woman recovering from a failed suicide attempt and the two begin a journey of mutual healing.

"Given the insanity of Japanese society today, where the main topics of conversation are extramarital love affairs or high school student prostitution... I thought it relevant to picture a man who doesn't regret killing his unfaithful wife," the filmmaker said in an interview prior to the win.

With the success of "Unagi" Imamura becomes a two-time Cannes winner, following his first Palme d'Or for "Narayama-bushi-ko" ("The Ballad of Narayama") in 1983, a feat accomplished by only three other top directors, including Francis Ford Coppola.
Imamura, who overcame diabetes to make "Unagi", made his first film, "Stolen Desire", in 1958 followed by "My Second Brother" and "The Insect Woman", both of which won critical acclaim abroad.
Japan also won the Cannes "Best New Director" prize, awarded to Naomi Kawase for her feature "Moe-no-Suzaku" (The God Suzaku), which focuses on family ties.

Coming before the June 27 American release of the Japanese hit film "Shall We Dance", which features Koji Yakusho, the leading actor in "Unagi", the two wins herald a new international image for Japanese films, said a spokesman for Japan Film Distribution Abroad.

"The Cannes win is very important because it's such a famous award. People know about the famous directors like Akira Kurosawa and Nagisa Oshima. But even though Japanese directors have been winning prizes in Berlin and London for the past 10 years, our presence has been slight," the spokesman said.
"Shall We Dance", a comedy which last year was Japan's top box office hit, features a bureaucrat who escapes from his humdrum existence when he discovers ballroom dancing.
